Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

17 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: the bird's head, its black cap against the sun's glow Light: a low sun at the upper right, behind the bird: warm light on the bird's chest and the top of the branchHow this lesson was made

What you need

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the misty sunset glowFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Pull down the far misty trunksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff brush: Dab the hazy rust foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch flat: Pull the branch and trunk in bark brownFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Block in the four leavesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #4 round: Shade the wing with warm grayRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #2 round: Stripe the wing feathersRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • liner: Add the eye and beakLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

All 13 paints and their recipes. Each step lists the ones it needs, so you can mix as you go

You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The four leaves; 2 The chickadee; 3 Legs and feet. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • X stroke, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Dry brush, first in step 3. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Dabbing, first in step 4.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 5.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 7.
  • Press and lift, first in step 8. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Liner work, first in step 16. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The misty glow 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 17 · The misty glow, 1 of 2

Blend the misty sunset glow

  1. Inside the outlined area: the whole canvas.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Sunset gold, then Misty blue-gray.
  3. Mix enough Sunset gold for this step and steps 8 and 9; cover it between them.
  4. Mix enough Misty blue-gray for this step and steps 3, 10 and 16; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: One or two colors on the brush. How much of each is on it controls the blend.
  6. Short strokes that cross each other in two directions, like overlapping X shapes.
  7. It should leave a soft, slightly textured blended fill with visible criss-cross marks.
  8. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  9. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes from a low sun in the upper right, behind the bird, so keep the gold brightest around that corner and let it run down through the middle of the canvas, fading to blue-gray toward the left, right, and bottom edges. While it's still wet, pull a few faint blue-gray streaks straight down at the left side and bottom middle for the farthest misty trunks. Blend straight across where the branch and bird will go; they go on top later.

STEP 2 OF 17 · The misty glow, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the misty sunset glow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 4 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 1 1/2 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
  4. Paint: Sun cream.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush, moving outward from the middle of the sun, give it a soft, bumpy edge.
  7. It should leave a bumpy, soft edge.
  8. Watch out: The edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter passes of small circles around the rim.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is a disc about 1 1/2 inches across, a little right of the canvas's middle, near the top. Keep its edge soft so it glows into the gold around it.

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.

The far woods 2 steps

STEP 3 OF 17 · The far woods, 1 of 2

Pull down the far misty trunks

  1. Let the misty glow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom to the right edge. Its left side is about 3 1/2 in from the right edge.
  3. Paints, darkest first: Dusky mauve, then Misty blue-gray. The paint map shows where each goes.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Watch out: Far trunks that look sharp and dark. Fix: keep the brush wiped nearly dry and the pressure light, so the mist shows through. These far trunks get no light pass.

Tip: Pull each trunk straight down from the top edge in one long stroke: two tall trunks side by side, and a fainter one to their left. They're far away in the mist, so let the gold and blue-gray show through.

STEP 4 OF 17 · The far woods, 2 of 2

Dab the hazy rust foliage

  1. Let the far misty trunks and the misty glow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Warm rust.
  4. Mix enough Warm rust for this step and steps 6 and 7; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: old stiff brush. Load: A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.
  6. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  7. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  8. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Tap the clumps in loose groups, thickest at the upper right and along the right and bottom, some over the trunks. Tap harder in the middle of each clump so it's solid and darker, and lightly at its edges so the glow shows through. Leave the gold glow around the sun and most of the blue-gray mist open.

The branch 2 steps

STEP 5 OF 17 · The branch, 1 of 2

Pull the branch and trunk in bark brown

  1. Let the far woods and the misty glow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Bark brown.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  5. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.
  6. It should leave a line that starts wide and tapers to a point: wide at the trunk, thin at the twig tips.
  7. Watch out: Branches that look like stiff sticks. Every branch the same width and straight. Fix: start thick at the trunk and taper. Let branches fork in different directions and overlap.

Tip: The trunk rises up the left side and the branch sweeps from the lower left corner in an arch to the lower right, like a bent bow. Pull each stroke along the branch, thick at the trunk end and thinner toward the twig tips; add the two thin twigs off its right end and the short stems to the leaves.

STEP 6 OF 17 · The branch, 2 of 2

Catch the light along the top of the bark

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. It reaches all four edges of the canvas.
  3. Paint: Warm rust.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 5 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Warm rust is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.
  10. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun is upper right, so the light catches the top of the branch and the right side of the trunk. Leave the bark brown showing underneath and along the bottom edge of the branch.

The leaves 2 steps

STEP 7 OF 17 · The leaves, 1 of 2

Block in the four leaves

  1. Let the branch and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge and its right side is about 3 in from the right edge.
  4. Paints, darkest first: Leaf red, then Warm rust. The paint map shows where each goes.
  5. Brush: #8 round.
  6. Start each leaf with its center as one pointed oval along its stem line. Then add the side lobes in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the tip.
  7. It should leave a shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Tip: Two leaves hang at the top left from the trunk's twig, and two hang under the branch at the lower right. The red ones are the lower of each pair; the other two are blocked in warm rust now and turn gold in the next step.

STEP 8 OF 17 · The leaves, 2 of 2

Light the leaves with gold

  1. Let the four leaves and the branch dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, top to bottom. Its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge and its right side is about 3 1/2 in from the right edge.
  3. Paint: Sunset gold.
  4. Brush: #6 round. Load: Creamy paint, a full load.
  5. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  6. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted.
  7. Leave what step 7 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Stroke from the stem out toward each leaf's edge. Cover most of the two upper leaves of each pair with gold, and only touch the red leaves' right edges, so they stay red. Pull a thin vein down each leaf's middle with the brush tip.

Feathers and face 5 steps

STEP 13 OF 17 · Feathers and face, 1 of 5

Feather the sunlit chest

  1. Let the chickadee's shape and the far woods dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 3/4 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 2 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 7 in wide and 5 1/2 in tall.
  3. Paint: Chest cream.
  4. Brush: 1/2 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  5. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  6. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  7. Leave what step 9 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Watch out: The feathers turn into a flat smooth patch. Too much paint on the brush, or the strokes are blended together.
  9. Fix: wipe the brush nearly dry, make each stroke short and separate, and let it dry before adding more.

Tip: The light is behind the bird on the right, so the cream goes on the right half of the chest and belly, under the bib. Stroke down and around the curve of the body, and leave the gold showing on the lower left of the belly. With what's left on the nearly dry brush, drag one or two light streaks along the top edge of the wing and the tail, so they catch a little light too.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved brown branch, with a few orange and yellow autumn leaves, in front of a soft, misty autumn forest with a low sun at the upper right.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The image is the painting edge to edge: no bars, text, border, watermark, or frame.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: About 11%: a thin strip of misty forest off each side (the trunk's far left edge and the far right background trees).

Why: No canvas was named, so fit-canvas picked the standard size closest to the 3:2 photo (12x16, landscape). A crop keeps the bird, its branch, and the hanging leaves whole, so no extend render was needed.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: no (the only things besides the bird are four big leaves, one branch with a few twigs, and soft blurred trunks). Textures of hundreds of items: no (the background foliage is soft blobs, not single leaves; busy outlined only 2 tiles, 0.4% of the canvas, at the wing tip over the tail and at the right foot on the branch, both small subject details, not texture). Detail inside big shapes one repeated mark can't make: no (the bark is short broken strokes, one repeated mark; the leaf veins are single lines; the wing's feather edges are the subject's own shading steps). More parts at different distances than the budget's 8: no (three distances: misty background with sun and trunks, the branch and leaves, the bird).

Changed: none

Why: The picture is already a loose, simple painting with a soft background and one clear subject, so a beginner version would only cost a render and risk changing the bird. busy agreed: 0.4% fine texture, the same as the spike's chickadee.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.4% of the canvas

A calm picture: one small bird on an arching branch against a soft, misty autumn wood with a low sun behind it. What matters is the glow (gold around the sun fading to blue-gray mist), the dark branch arch that holds the composition, and the chickadee's crisp black cap and bib against that glow. The hard part for a beginner is the bird: a round body, a sharply edged cap and bib, and small details (eye, beak, toes). The lesson should be about painting a soft background and then a crisp subject on top of it.

Subject: A black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch
Focal point: the bird's head, its black cap against the sun's glow
Light: a low sun at the upper right, behind the bird: warm light on the bird's chest and the top of the branch

What it saw, back to front

  1. Misty sunset glow
  2. The branch
  3. The four leaves
  4. The chickadee
  5. Legs and feet
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front fits exactly: blend the whole misty background wet, add the far trunks and hazy foliage, then the branch, the leaves, and the bird on top, each over the one behind. It's the beginner approach and the only technique with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It has no version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules), so pipeline v2 can't plan with it; and a paint-along suits this soft background better than flat block-in shapes.

How the paint recipes were worked out13 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Misty blue-gray Delta E 5.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Sunset gold Delta E 0.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts red

  • Sun cream Delta E 1.3
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 1 part yellow, a touch of red

  • Dusky mauve Delta E 2.0
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 3 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts ultramarine, a touch of yellow

  • Warm rust Delta E 2.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts white, 1 part red, a touch of yellow

  • Bark brown Delta E 1.9
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part red, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of yellow

  • Leaf red Delta E 2.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts red, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of white

  • Chest cream Delta E 2.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 4 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Pale feather gray Delta E 2.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

  • Warm wing gray Delta E 3.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts burnt sienna, 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine, a touch of yellow

  • Chickadee black Delta E 3.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Cheek white Delta E 1.3
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow, a touch of ultramarine

  • Leg gray Delta E 5.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of yellow

Furthest off: Delta E 5.8. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order17 steps

Back to front: the glow and sun first, then the far trunks and the foliage in front of them, then the near branch, the leaves hanging from it, and the bird sitting on it. Inside the bird: the body coat, the wing and tail over it, the cap and bib, the cheek between them, then the light chest, the wing shading and stripes, and the eye, beak, and feet last, over the dry branch.

  1. 1. Blend the misty sunset glow

    The whole background is one wet blend from gold to blue-gray; it goes first so everything else sits on it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    The sun is on the background, the brightest spot; painted once the glow is dry so its edge stays soft but clean.

  3. 3. Pull down the far misty trunks

    The farthest things in front of the mist; dry-brushed so they stay hazy, before the foliage that overlaps them.

  4. 4. Dab the hazy rust foliage

    The far autumn clumps sit in front of the trunks, so they go on after them, still before anything near.

  5. 5. Pull the branch and trunk in bark brown

    The branch is the nearest big shape behind the bird and leaves: its dark coat goes on before what hangs from or sits on it.

  6. 6. Catch the light along the top of the bark

    The second value on the branch: light on the top facing the sun, over the dry dark coat.

  7. 7. Block in the four leaves

    The leaves hang in front of the background and from the branch, so after the branch; blocked in from pieces first.

  8. 8. Light the leaves with gold

    The leaves' light side, gold, over the dry block-in: the second value, toward the sun.

  9. 9. Block in the round body

    The subject goes on last of the big shapes; its body coat first, as one plump shape.

  10. 10. Block in the wing and tail

    The wing and tail lie over the body, so they go on its dry coat.

  11. 11. Paint the black cap and bib

    The black cap and bib are the subject's strongest darks; one shape built from two pieces, over the body.

  12. 12. Paint the white cheek

    The white cheek fits between the cap and bib, so after them.

  13. 13. Feather the sunlit chest

    The light on the chest facing the sun: the body's lighter value, over the dry gold.

  14. 14. Shade the wing with warm gray

    A first shading pass on the wing's lower feather edges, before the darkest stripes.

  15. 15. Stripe the wing feathers

    The darkest feather stripes, over the dry wing, after the lighter shading.

  16. 16. Add the eye and beak

    The eye and beak are the smallest details: liner work over the dry head, near the end.

  17. 17. Add the legs and toes

    The legs and toes cross over the branch and the bird's belly, so they go on last, over both dry.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • busy (#109) measured the fitted photo at 0.4% fine texture (2 tiles, the wing tip over the tail and the right foot), matching the spike's chickadee number and my own read: no beginner version.
  • The first finish came back from the render cache (an earlier run had made it from the same reference and photo) with the mist a bright saturated blue; the one fix render matched the photo.
  • paints --add is not free: adding a color for the wing pushed the count to 11 and the rerun it asked for merged Slate gray into Misty blue-gray. The added wing color (#89776d) was a warm brownish gray, not the light feather edge I wanted, so the wing has no light pass.
  • paints --add bird (for a darker belly shade) measured a pale gray (#a29b9c), not a darker gold; a pass with it changed almost nothing and was taken out, but the paint can't be deleted by hand, so Pale feather gray stays in the plan unused and the lesson counts 11 base mixes.
  • The far trunks' marks outline took wavy blobs of mist beside the trunks; two rounds of points only helped partly. The eye and beak outline shows in the cap, cheek, and chest pictures before its own step (78% of its edge, 44% after loosening the boxes).
  • Card lines rewritten for this subject: small-circles (sun, not a cloud), the trunks-branches watch-out (far misty trunks), thick-to-thin result (trunk and twig tips), build-from-pieces (leaves, body, wing, cap and bib, cheek), liner (eye and beak, legs and toes, not branches), and the feathered-body fix line (dry brush, not flicks).
